dryRun.title: Kruskal's algorithm. Edges (weight): 0-1 (1), 1-2 (2), 0-2 (3), 2-3 (4), 1-3 (5), tried from the lightest
rows: yes: 0 and 2 are already joined through 1
dryRun.note: A minimum spanning tree joins all n nodes with n - 1 edges and the smallest possible total weight. Kruskal: go through edges from the lightest, and take an edge only if it joins two different groups (union-find).

think.q:
const edges = [[0, 1, 1], [1, 2, 2], [0, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [1, 3, 5]]
edges.sort((a, b) => a[2] - b[2])
const parent = [0, 1, 2, 3]
const find = (x) => (parent[x] === x ? x : (parent[x] = find(parent[x])))
let total = 0, used = 0
for (const [u, v, w] of edges) {
  const a = find(u), b = find(v)
  if (a !== b) { parent[b] = a; total += w; used++ }
}
console.log(total, used)
why: The edges 0-1, 1-2 and 2-3 are taken (1 + 2 + 4 = 7). The others join nodes that are already in one group. 4 nodes need exactly 3 edges.
The a !== b test is the cycle check.

think.q: A connected graph has 10 nodes. How many edges does its minimum spanning tree have?
why: A tree on n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges: fewer would leave a node out, and more would make a cycle.
If the algorithm ends with fewer than n - 1 edges, the graph is not connected.

think.q: Why is it safe to take the lightest edge that does not make a cycle?
opts: Because lighter edges are always shorter
The lightest edge crossing any split of the nodes always belongs to some minimum spanning tree (the cut property)
It is not safe, Kruskal is only a guess
why: Imagine splitting the nodes into two sides. The cheapest edge between the sides can always be swapped into an optimal tree without making it worse.
This is the exchange-argument idea from the greedy lesson.

think.q: What is the difference between Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms?
opts: Kruskal sorts all edges and joins groups; Prim grows one tree from a start node, always adding the cheapest edge leaving it (with a heap)
Prim is for directed graphs only
Kruskal uses a queue and Prim uses a stack
why: Both give a tree with the same minimum total weight. Kruskal suits an edge list, Prim suits an adjacency list and dense graphs.
Kruskal is O(E log E) because of the sort.

think.q: Is the minimum spanning tree always unique?
opts: The total weight is unique, but the tree can differ when several edges have the same weight
No, even the total can differ
Only when the graph is a tree
why: If all weights are different, the tree is unique. With ties, several trees may share the same minimum total.
That is why tests compare the total weight, not the exact edges.

try.task: Write mstWeight(n, edges). The graph is undirected with nodes 0 to n - 1, and each edge is [a, b, weight]. Return the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, or -1 if the graph is not connected. A graph with one node has weight 0.
try.hint: Sort a copy of the edges by weight. Use union-find (an iterative find). Take an edge when its two ends have different roots. If you took fewer than n - 1 edges, return -1.

checks.t: a graph that is not connected
a cheaper path replaces a heavy edge

checks.verify: const e = [[0, 1, 4], [0, 2, 1]]; mstWeight(3, e); assert(JSON.stringify(e) === "[[0,1,4],[0,2,1]]", "the input was changed")

takeaway.key: A minimum spanning tree connects all nodes with n - 1 edges at the least total weight. Kruskal: sort the edges and take each one that joins two different groups (union-find). O(E log E).
mistakes: Not noticing the graph is disconnected (fewer than n - 1 edges taken).
Sorting the caller's array in place.
Mixing up MST with shortest paths (they are different problems).

dryRun.title: Bellman-Ford from node 0. Edges in this order: 0→1 (4), 0→2 (5), 2→1 (-3), 1→3 (2)
rows: nothing changes, so we can stop
dryRun.note: Instead of being clever about the order, just relax every edge, and repeat. After pass k, every shortest path using at most k edges is correct. A shortest path has at most V - 1 edges, so V - 1 passes are enough.

think.q:
const n = 4
const edges = [[0, 1, 4], [0, 2, 5], [2, 1, -3], [1, 3, 2]]
const dist = Array(n).fill(Infinity)
dist[0] = 0
for (let pass = 0; pass < n - 1; pass++) {
  for (const [u, v, w] of edges) {
    if (dist[u] + w < dist[v]) dist[v] = dist[u] + w
  }
}
console.log(dist.join(","))
why: The cheapest way to node 1 is 0 → 2 → 1 = 5 - 3 = 2, and then node 3 costs 2 + 2 = 4.
Dijkstra could go wrong here, because the edge 2→1 is negative.

think.q:
const n = 3
const edges = [[0, 1, 1], [1, 2, -3], [2, 1, 1]]
const dist = Array(n).fill(Infinity)
dist[0] = 0
for (let pass = 0; pass < n - 1; pass++) {
  for (const [u, v, w] of edges) if (dist[u] + w < dist[v]) dist[v] = dist[u] + w
}
let again = false
for (const [u, v, w] of edges) if (dist[u] + w < dist[v]) again = true
console.log(again)
why: The loop 1 → 2 → 1 costs -3 + 1 = -2 each time round, so distances could shrink forever. After n - 1 passes an edge can still be relaxed, which proves a negative cycle.
If the extra pass changes nothing, there is no negative cycle that you can reach.

think.q: Why are V - 1 passes enough when there is no negative cycle?
opts: Because V - 1 is a lucky number
A shortest path never repeats a node, so it has at most V - 1 edges, and each pass fixes one more edge of every path
Because each pass visits one node
why: After pass 1 all shortest paths of 1 edge are right, after pass 2 all of 2 edges, and so on up to V - 1.
You can stop early when a whole pass changes nothing.

think.q: What is the time of Bellman-Ford?
why: V - 1 passes, each over E edges. That is slower than Dijkstra's O((V + E) log V).
You pay that price only to get negative weights and cycle detection.

think.q: Prices can go up and down, and you want to find a loop of trades that makes a profit (arbitrage). Which algorithm fits?
opts: Bellman-Ford, looking for a negative cycle on log-prices
why: A profitable loop is a cycle whose total (log) weight is negative. Bellman-Ford detects exactly that.
Dijkstra needs non-negative weights, so it cannot be used here.

try.task: Write bellmanFord(n, edges, start). The graph is directed; each edge is [from, to, weight] and weights may be negative. Return the array of shortest distances from start (Infinity if unreachable). If a negative cycle can be reached from start, return null.
try.hint: Repeat n - 1 times: for each edge, if dist[u] is not Infinity and dist[u] + w < dist[v], update. Then run one more pass: any update means a negative cycle, so return null.

checks.verify: const d = bellmanFord(3, [[0, 1, 2]], 0); assert(d[2] === Infinity && d[1] === 2, "expected Infinity for node 2")

checks.t: a negative cycle that cannot be reached is ignored
checks.verify: const d = bellmanFord(4, [[0, 1, 1], [2, 3, -5], [3, 2, 1]], 0); assert(d !== null && d[1] === 1 && d[2] === Infinity, "the unreachable cycle must not matter")
const d2 = bellmanFord(2, [], 1); assert(d2[0] === Infinity && d2[1] === 0, "expected [Infinity, 0]")

takeaway.key: Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge V - 1 times, so it handles negative weights. One extra pass that still improves something means a negative cycle. Time O(V × E).
mistakes: Using Dijkstra when a weight is negative.
Relaxing from a node whose distance is still Infinity (Infinity + a negative number is still Infinity, but be careful to keep the guard).
Reporting a negative cycle that is not reachable from the start.

dryRun.title: Floyd-Warshall on 3 nodes with edges 0→1 (3), 1→2 (1), 0→2 (8). Each round k allows node k as a stop-over
dryRun.note: The idea: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]). After round k, every distance is the best one that only uses the nodes 0 to k as stop-overs. The k loop must be outermost.

think.q:
const n = 3, INF = Infinity
const d = [[0, 3, 8], [INF, 0, 1], [INF, INF, 0]]
for (let k = 0; k < n; k++)
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (let j = 0; j < n; j++)
      if (d[i][k] + d[k][j] < d[i][j]) d[i][j] = d[i][k] + d[k][j]
console.log(JSON.stringify(d[0]))
why: The direct edge 0→2 costs 8, but 0→1→2 costs 3 + 1 = 4. When k = 1 the code finds it.
JSON writes Infinity as null; here row 0 has no infinity, so it prints clean numbers.

think.q: Which loop must be the outermost in Floyd-Warshall, and why?
opts: i, because it is the start node
j, because it is the end node
k, the stop-over: the table after round k must be fully correct for stop-overs 0 to k before we allow k + 1
why: The meaning of the table depends on k. If k is not the outer loop, the pieces d[i][k] and d[k][j] may not be final yet.
This is the most common mistake with this algorithm.

think.q: What are the time and the space of Floyd-Warshall for V nodes?
why: Three nested loops over V give V³. The table has V × V cells.
That is fine up to a few hundred nodes, and too slow beyond a thousand.

think.q: After the algorithm finishes, how can you see that a negative cycle exists?
why: The distance from a node to itself should be 0. If a negative loop through it exists, going round gives a smaller number.
Like Bellman-Ford, it can detect negative cycles.

think.q: You need the distance between every pair of 200 cities. Which approach is simplest?
why: 200³ = 8 million, which is instant. It is short to write and handles negative edges.
For a huge sparse graph, running Dijkstra from each node can be better.

try.task: Write allPairs(n, edges). The graph is directed; each edge is [from, to, weight] (weights are 0 or more). Return an n × n matrix d where d[i][j] is the shortest distance from i to j, with d[i][i] = 0 and Infinity when there is no path.
try.hint: Fill the matrix with Infinity, the diagonal with 0, then each edge (keep the smaller weight if there are several). Then three loops with k outermost.

checks.t: a shorter way through a middle node

checks.verify: const d = allPairs(2, []); assert(d[0][0] === 0 && d[0][1] === Infinity && d[1][0] === Infinity && d[1][1] === 0, "expected zeros on the diagonal and Infinity elsewhere")

checks.t: the cheaper of two parallel edges

checks.verify: const d = allPairs(2, [[0, 1, 5]]); assert(d[0][1] === 5 && d[1][0] === Infinity, "the edge only goes one way")

const n = 150; const e = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => [i, (i + 1) % n, 1]); const d = allPairs(n, e); let ok = true; for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 7) for (let j = 0; j < n; j += 5) if (d[i][j] !== (j - i + n) % n) ok = false; assert(ok, "a distance in the ring is wrong")

takeaway.key: Floyd-Warshall finds all-pairs shortest paths with three loops, k outermost: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]). O(V³) time, O(V²) space. A negative d[i][i] means a negative cycle.
mistakes: Putting k in the inner loop.
Overwriting a parallel edge with a heavier one.
Using it on thousands of nodes.

dryRun.title: Hierholzer's algorithm on a directed graph with edges 0→1, 1→2, 2→0, 0→3, 3→0
columns: next unused edge from the top
dryRun.note: Walk along unused edges until you are stuck, then pop nodes into the path. Reverse the path at the end. Every edge is used exactly once, so the time is O(E).

think.q:
const adj = { 0: [1, 3], 1: [2], 2: [0], 3: [0] }
const stack = [0], path = []
while (stack.length) {
  const u = stack[stack.length - 1]
  if (adj[u].length) stack.push(adj[u].shift())
  else path.push(stack.pop())
}
console.log(path.reverse().join(","))
why: The walk follows 0→1→2→0→3→0, uses all five edges, and gets stuck at 0. Then every node is popped into the path.
Reversing the popped order gives the circuit in the right direction.

think.q:
const edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0], [2, 3]]
const deg = [0, 0, 0, 0]
for (const [a, b] of edges) { deg[a]++; deg[b]++ }
console.log(deg.filter((d) => d % 2 === 1).length)
why: The degrees are 2, 2, 3 and 1. Nodes 2 and 3 have an odd degree, so there are two odd nodes.
In an undirected connected graph, 0 odd nodes means an Euler circuit, exactly 2 means an Euler path (start at one odd node, end at the other), and any other count means neither exists.
think.exec:
const edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0], [2, 3]]
const deg = [0, 0, 0, 0]
for (const [a, b] of edges) { deg[a]++; deg[b]++ }
console.log(deg.filter((d) => d % 2 === 1).length)

think.q: What does an Euler path visit exactly once, compared with a Hamiltonian path?
opts: Euler: every node once. Hamiltonian: every edge once
Euler: every edge once. Hamiltonian: every node once
why: Euler is about edges and is easy to decide with degrees. Hamiltonian is about nodes and is NP-hard.
This is a classic interview question, and the Königsberg bridges are the origin story.

think.q: When does a directed graph (with all edges in one connected piece) have an Euler circuit?
opts: When every node has in-degree equal to out-degree
When every node has an even total degree
When it has a node with no edges
why: Every time you arrive at a node you must be able to leave it, so the arrivals and departures must match.
For an Euler path exactly one node has out - in = 1 (the start) and one has in - out = 1 (the end).

think.q: What is the time of Hierholzer's algorithm for a graph with E edges?
why: Each edge is taken off a list once and each node push has a matching pop. (Remove edges by moving an index, not with shift(), to keep it linear.)
Trying all orders by backtracking would be exponential, so this algorithm is a big improvement.

try.task: Write eulerCircuit(edges). edges is a list of directed edges [from, to]. Return a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once, as a list of nodes starting at edges[0][0] (so it has edges.length + 1 nodes). Return [] if there are no edges or no such circuit exists.
try.hint: First check that every node has in-degree equal to out-degree. Then run Hierholzer with an index pointer per node instead of shift(). If the final path has fewer than edges.length + 1 nodes, the edges are not all connected: return [].

checks.t: a valid circuit uses every edge once
checks.verify: const edges = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [2, 0], [0, 3], [3, 0]]; const p = eulerCircuit(edges); assert(p.length === 6 && p[0] === 0 && p[5] === 0, "expected 6 nodes that start and end at 0"); const used = p.slice(0, -1).map((u, i) => u + ">" + p[i + 1]).sort(); const want = edges.map(([a, b]) => a + ">" + b).sort(); assert(JSON.stringify(used) === JSON.stringify(want), "every edge must be used exactly once")

checks.t: a path that is not closed
two separate cycles can not be walked

checks.verify: const n = 100000; const e = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => [i, (i + 1) % n]); const t0 = Date.now(); const p = eulerCircuit(e); assert(p.length === n + 1 && p[0] === 0 && p[n] === 0 && Date.now() - t0 < 1000, "wrong circuit or too slow")

takeaway.key: An Euler path uses every edge once. Check the degrees first (even degrees for a circuit in an undirected graph, in = out for a directed one), then use Hierholzer: walk until stuck, pop into the path, reverse. O(E).
mistakes: Skipping the degree check or the "all edges connected" check.
Forgetting to reverse the popped path.

flags: euler-path: the try-it accepts any valid circuit (checks length, start/end and that every edge is used once), since many circuits exist.
floyd-warshall: the ring check samples every 7th row and 5th column of the 150 x 150 result to keep the script light.
The dry-run tables are traced by hand (concept dry runs are not machine-run).
